# Somatic symptom and related disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Psychiatric disorders > Somatic symptom and related disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/MP0M2T)

---

## Summary

Somatic symptom and related disorders are characterized by prominent somatic symptoms associated with significant <u>distress</u> and psychosocial impairment, and cannot be fully explained by a recognized medical condition. Somatic symptoms may be also present in patients with a known medical condition (e.g., <u>psychogenic nonepileptic seizures</u> in patients with <u>epilepsy</u>). The absence of a medical explanation should not imply that the patient's symptoms are not genuine or that they can consciously control their symptoms. Personal <u>stress</u>, <u>depression</u>, and interpersonal conflicts often exacerbate these disorders; however, psychological stressors are not always evident and may not be significant even when present. More than half of all primary care visits are related to somatic symptom and related disorders, however, diagnosis can be challenging, as it is primarily a diagnosis of exclusion. Management of somatic symptom and related disorders involves patient education and <u>psychotherapy</u>. It is crucial to schedule regular visits with the same physician to avoid unnecessary tests and procedures. Rarely, symptoms may be intentionally induced, invented, or exaggerated either for <u>primary gain</u> (<u>factitious disorder</u>) or <u>secondary gain</u> (<u>malingering</u>). Management of these patients is extremely challenging and involves carefully planned and coordinated intervention.

---

## Etiology

### <u>Risk factors</u> [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




The following <u>risk factors</u> are commonly found in patients with somatic symptom and related disorders:




* Psychiatric disorders (e.g., <u>depression</u>, <u>personality disorder</u>)

* Concurrent physical illness (especially comorbid neurological illness in <u>functional neurological disorder</u>)

* <u>Gender</u>: <u>Incidence</u> is higher in women than men.  [[2]](/library/LGcw-d0)

* Low <u>socioeconomic status</u>

* History of:

* <u>Sexual abuse</u>

* Childhood abuse

* Recent stressful life event

---

## Conditions in which symptoms are unconsciously generated

* In the majority of somatic symptom and related disorders:

* Symptoms are not intentionally induced or invented (unlike in <u>factitious disorders</u> or <u>malingering</u>).

* Patients are distressed by their symptoms and seek a diagnosis and treatment.

* There is no deliberate attempt to deceive others, including health care staff.

---

## Diagnostic approach and general management

### Diagnostic approach [[3]](/library/pNXLXA)[[4]](/library/rkcf6c0)




* Review the patient's medical record and consider contacting any specialists the patient has consulted in the past.

* Perform a detailed history and <u>physical examination</u> including the following aspects:

* Diagnostic studies to rule out a treatable medical condition

* Empathic interview techniques using a <u>trauma-informed approach</u>

* <u>Risk factors</u> in the patient's history (e.g., history of childhood abuse/neglect or <u>sexual abuse</u>, past psychiatric diagnoses).

* Cultural context (see “<u>Culture in the health care setting</u>” for more information).

* Ask the patient how their symptoms may be affecting their mood.  [[4]](/library/rkcf6c0)

* Consider using screening tools. 

* Patient health questionnaire-15 (<u>PHQ-15</u>)

* The somatic symptom scale-8 is an abbreviated version of the <u>PHQ-15</u> that evaluates the severity of eight somatic symptoms in a 7-day time frame. [[5]](/library/Lqcw_W0)

* <u>DSM-5</u> criteria must be met to reach a diagnosis of a somatic symptom and related disorder.





> [!WARNING]
> Performing extensive diagnostic studies, which are often inconclusive, in patients in whom there is no indication of a medical condition may result in higher levels of patient frustration and excessive health care costs. [[4]](/library/rkcf6c0)




> [!TIP]
> Apply the BATHE technique to assess for psychosocial factors: Background: “What is going on in your life at the moment?,” Affect: “How does that make you feel?,” Trouble: “What is the most difficult part of this situation?,” Handling: “How are you managing that?,” Empathy: “This must be very challenging for you.” [[4]](/library/rkcf6c0)




![Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15)](media/ap0br042w7mxrvcg689dsy5i.jpg)

Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15)




### General principles of management [[3]](/library/pNXLXA)[[4]](/library/rkcf6c0)[[6]](/library/VkcG5c0)




* Challenges can strain the <u>patient-physician relationship</u> and reduce the quality of care.

* Management of somatic symptoms can be emotionally challenging for clinicians.

* Patients may become hostile or aggressive in response to a perceived stigmatizing diagnosis.

* Patients may make a complaint against the clinician.

* See “<u>Anger and threats from patients</u>” for further information.

* Patient education

* Involve the patient in the diagnostic and management process.

* Ask about their expectations from management.

* Ask what they think may be causing their symptoms.

* Explain the diagnosis to the patient.

* Acknowledge symptoms and explain the results of the <u>physical examination</u> and diagnostic studies.

* Educate patients on <u>brain</u>-body interactions and provide examples of:

* Psychologically generated symptoms (e.g., racing <u>heart</u> and sweating palms when nervous)

* Common conditions that are affected by psychological factors (e.g., <u>dyspepsia</u>, <u>hypertension</u>).

* Emphasize that symptoms are potentially reversible and reassure the patient that it is unlikely that they have a serious illness.

* Reassure the patient that somatic symptom and related disorders are recognized conditions and that their symptoms are not perceived to be fictitious.

* Medical management

* Minimize unnecessary studies and procedures

* Schedule regular visits with the same primary care physician

* Coordinate with other <u>health care professionals</u> who the patient may be consulting

* Help avoid potential <u>doctor shopping</u>.

* Review symptom severity (consider using screening tools) and perform a <u>physical examination</u> at every visit.

* Avoid medication prescriptions, study requests, and patient referrals if they are not needed.

* Psychological and psychiatric management

* <u>Psychotherapy</u>: primarily <u>cognitive behavior therapy</u>  [[6]](/library/VkcG5c0)

* Consider prescribing an <u>antidepressant</u> (typically an <u>SNRI</u>, <u>SSRI</u>, or tricyclic).  [[3]](/library/pNXLXA)[[4]](/library/rkcf6c0)

* Treat comorbid psychiatric conditions (e.g., <u>depression</u>, <u>anxiety</u>).  [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Consider a <u>psychiatry</u> consultation.  [[7]](/library/5OciGc0)





> [!TIP]
> Remember the CARE-MD approach for patients with somatic symptoms: Consult with <u>psychiatry</u>/Cognitive <u>behavior therapy</u>, Assess for comorbid diseases, Regular visits, Empathy (<u>trauma-informed approach</u>), explain the Medical and psychiatric interface, Do not harm (avoid unnecessary tests and referrals). [[3]](/library/pNXLXA)

---

## Somatic symptom disorder

### Overview




* Individuals with <u>somatic symptom disorder</u> often have:

* Multiple physical symptoms that cause significant <u>distress</u>

* A history of extensive (and fruitless) diagnostic testing and medical procedures

* A preoccupation with their symptoms and health concerns for ≥ 6 months

* Symptoms may be related to an existing medical condition.





### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>

* <u>Prevalence</u> in adults: ∼ 5–7% [[3]](/library/pNXLXA)





### Diagnostics




* Clinical and diagnostic study results cannot be fully explained by a recognized medical condition.

* Screening tools may identify patients at risk for <u>somatic symptom disorder</u>.

* All of the following <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria must be met: [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

* ≥ 1 somatic symptom (e.g., <u>heartburn</u>, fatigue, <u>headache</u>, <u>pain</u>) that causes significant <u>distress</u> or impairment

* Excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to the somatic symptoms or health concerns, manifesting as ≥ 1 of the following:

* Disproportionate and constant thoughts of symptom severity

* Constant and significant <u>anxiety</u> about symptoms or general health

* Excessive amounts of time and energy spent attending to symptoms or health concerns

* Duration: ≥ 6 months





> [!TIP]
> Some patients may present with only one severe symptom, most commonly <u>pain</u>. [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




### Management




See “<u>Approach to patients with suspected somatic symptom and related disorders</u>” for more information.




* Minimize unnecessary studies and procedures.

* Schedule regular visits with the same primary care physician.

* <u>Psychotherapy</u>: primarily <u>cognitive behavior therapy</u>





> [!TIP]
> Patients with <u>somatic symptom disorder</u> often visit multiple physicians.

---

## Functional neurological symptom disorder

### Overview




* <u>Functional neurological symptom disorder</u> was formerly known as <u>conversion disorder</u>.

* Patients present with neurological symptoms that cannot be fully explained by a neurological condition.

* Patients may be calm and unconcerned when describing their symptoms (sometimes referred to as “la belle indifférence”).





> [!WARNING]
> A perceived lack of concern about symptoms is not specific to <u>functional neurological symptom disorder</u> and should not be used to confirm the diagnosis. [[8]](/library/Lebwzs)




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>

* Age of onset: ∼ 10–35 years of age [[9]](/library/USYb_o)





### Clinical features [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)[[10]](/library/64cj4c0)




* Patients may present with motor and/or sensory deficits affecting single or multiple areas of the body.

* Some clinical features are more commonly found in <u>functional neurological symptom disorder</u> than in neurological conditions.





| <br>Overview of common <u>physical examination</u> findings in <u>functional neurological symptom disorder</u> [[6]](/library/VkcG5c0)[[10]](/library/64cj4c0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Symptom | <br>Typical findings<br> |  |
| <br>Functional paralysis [[11]](/library/qGcCZV0)<br> | <br><br>* Normal <u>deep tendon reflexes</u><br><br>* <u>Paralysis</u> does not follow anatomical patterns.<br><br>* Arm <u>weakness</u><br><br>* Drift without <u>pronation</u> [[12]](/library/JGcsZV0)<br><br>* Positive <u>finger abduction test</u><br><br>* Leg <u>weakness</u><br><br>* Positive <u>Hoover sign</u><br><br>* Positive <u>hip abductor sign</u><br><br>* Dragging gait<br><br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures</u> [[13]](/library/KGcUZV0)<br> | <br><br>* Prolonged <u>seizures</u><br><br>* During <u>seizures</u><br><br>* Crying<br><br>* Head movement from side to side<br><br>* Clenching the eyes shut<br><br>* Hip thrusting<br><br>* <u>Tongue</u> biting: more commonly on the tip of the <u>tongue</u> than the sides<br><br>* Injuries, loss of <u>bladder</u> or bowel control, and <u>postictal</u> confusion are uncommon.<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Functional <u>dystonia</u> [[14]](/library/6GcjZV0)<br> | <br><br>* Sudden and rapid progression<br><br>* Typically manifests with a clenched fist or an inverted foot<br><br>* Severe <u>pain</u> is common.<br><br>* Symptoms do not improve with <u>sleep</u>.<br><br>* Often has atypical triggers (e.g., a loud noise)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Functional tremor</u> [[15]](/library/pGcLZV0)<br> | <br><br>* Sudden onset<br><br>* Varying location, frequency, amplitude, and/or direction<br><br>* <u>Tremor</u> reduces or changes with distraction.<br><br>* <u>Tremor</u> worsens if weights are attached to the limb.<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Functional vision disorder [[16]](/library/oGc0ZV0)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Pupillary reflex</u> present<br><br>* No signs of injury (e.g., <u>bruises</u> or scrapes) elsewhere on the body.<br><br>* <u>Visual acuity</u> unchanged by reduction of distance from the <u>eye</u> chart<br><br>* Optokinetic drum elicits <u>nystagmus</u>.<br><br>* Unable to direct gaze toward own hand or connect tips of own index fingers<br><br><br> |  |
| Functional <u>hearing loss</u> | <br>* Patients blink in response to loud sounds.<br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> Inconsistent examination findings are common in <u>functional neurological symptom disorder</u>; signs elicited during one examination may not always be present when using a different method.




### Diagnostics




* Thorough clinical assessment

* Evaluate the patient for common <u>physical examination</u> findings.

* Consider additional studies (e.g., <u>EEG</u>, <u>CT scan</u>, <u>nerve conduction studies</u>) and <u>neurology</u> consultation.

* All of the following <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria must be met: [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

* ≥ 1 neurological symptom (altered motor or <u>sensory function</u>): e.g., <u>paralysis</u>, muscle spasms, blindness, <u>mutism</u>, lump in throat, <u>weakness</u>, gait disorder

* Clinical features:

* Are incompatible with any recognized neurological or medical condition

* Cannot be better explained by another medical disorder

* Symptoms cause significant <u>distress</u> or psychosocial impairment or require medical evaluation





> [!TIP]
> Patients with neurological conditions (e.g., <u>epilepsy</u>, <u>Parkinson disease</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>) can present with concomitant <u>functional neurological symptom disorder</u>. [[10]](/library/64cj4c0)




> [!WARNING]
> Neurological disorders can manifest atypically, particularly in the early stages. Ensure appropriate diagnostic studies are performed and be prepared to revisit a diagnosis of <u>functional neurological symptom disorder</u> if symptoms worsen. [[17]](/library/rGcf0V0)




### Management [[18]](/library/-zdDvs0)




* Provide patient education

* If present, ensure comorbid neurological conditions are well-managed.

* <u>Physical therapy</u> can help reduce symptoms and prevent secondary complications of inactivity .

* Consider <u>psychotherapy</u> (e.g., <u>cognitive-behavioral therapy</u>)

* See “<u>Approach to patients with suspected somatic symptom and related disorders</u>” for more information.

## Illness anxiety disorder

### Overview




* Previously known as <u>hypochondriasis</u>

* Persistent preoccupation with having or developing a serious illness despite no concerning findings on multiple medical examinations

* Somatic symptoms are usually absent or mild, but patients spend large amounts of time and energy obsessing over their health and the possibility of developing a disease.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Illness anxiety disorder</u> in older patients is often focused on <u>memory</u> loss. [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>♀</u> = <u>♂</u> [[9]](/library/USYb_o)

* <u>Prevalence</u>: 1.3–10% [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

* A personal or <u>family history</u> of severe illness during the patient's childhood is common. [[19]](/library/NOc-sc0)





### Diagnosis [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




* No evidence of the illness of concern

* All the following <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria must be met: [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Preoccupation with having or developing an illness

* Absent or mild somatic symptoms

* Significant <u>anxiety</u> about health

* The patient exhibits: 

* Excessive health-related behaviors (e.g., constantly checking for signs of illness)

* OR incongruent avoidance behaviors (e.g., avoiding <u>screening tests</u>, doctor's appointments, attending hospital)

* Duration: ≥ 6 months

* Symptoms are not better explained by another mental disorder.





### Management




See “<u>Approach to patients with suspected somatic symptom and related disorders</u>” for more information.




* Minimize unnecessary studies and procedures

* Schedule regular visits with the same primary care physician

* <u>Psychotherapy</u>: primarily <u>cognitive behavior therapy</u>

---

## Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions

### Overview




* Definition: psychological or behavioral factors (such as maladaptive coping styles or <u>distress</u>) that adversely affect a medical condition by increasing the risk of severe symptoms, disability, or <u>death</u>

* Most medical conditions can be affected by psychological and/or behavioral factors

* Conditions with clear pathophysiology (e.g., <u>CAD</u>, <u>diabetes</u>)

* Functional syndromes (e.g., <u>IBS</u>, <u>fibromyalgia</u>)

* <u>Idiopathic</u> medical symptoms (e.g., <u>pain</u>, <u>vertigo</u>)





### Diagnostics




All of the following <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria must be met: [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




* A confirmed medical symptom or condition (that is not a mental disorder)

* The psychological and/or behavioral factors adversely affect one or more of the following aspects of the medical condition:

* The course of illness (e.g., failing to seek medical assistance when experiencing <u>acute chest pain</u>)

* The treatment of the condition (e.g., <u>poor adherence</u> to prescribed medication)

* Addition of further <u>risk factors</u> (e.g., a patient with <u>asthma</u> who starts smoking)

* The underlying pathophysiology or clinical features (e.g., chronic <u>stress</u> increasing the severity of <u>hypertension</u>)

* The psychological and/or behavioral factors are not better explained by another mental disorder.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions</u> should be differentiated from an <u>adjustment disorder</u>, in which symptoms affect the patient's mood but do not worsen their medical condition. [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




> [!TIP]
> Consider the patient's cultural context and establish how the patient perceives their condition before diagnosing <u>psychological factors affecting other medical conditions</u>.




### Management




* Treat the underlying medical condition and provide patient education.

* See “<u>Approach to patients with suspected somatic symptom and related disorders</u>.”

## Pseudocyesis

* Definition: the false belief of being pregnant associated with physical signs and <u>symptoms of pregnancy</u> without the presence of a fetus [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

* <u>Epidemiology</u>

* Peak age: typically 16–39 years of age [[20]](/library/HGcK0V0)

* More common in women who wish to and have a history of failure to conceive

* Etiology: not fully understood

* Somatopsychic hypothesis: body changes (e.g., abdominal distention due to <u>constipation</u>) are misinterpreted as signs of <u>pregnancy</u>, stimulating the psychosomatic development of further signs and symptoms [[21]](/library/Vc1GYf0)

* Psychophysiologic hypothesis: alterations in <u>neurotransmitters</u> are involved in the development of <u>pseudocyesis</u> [[22]](/library/dc1oYf0)

* Clinical features [[20]](/library/HGcK0V0)

* <u>Breast</u> tenderness, <u>hyperpigmentation</u> of the <u>nipples</u> and <u>areolas</u>

* Weight gain

* Menstrual irregularities

* <u>Morning sickness</u>

* Mild abdominal enlargement

* Sensation of fetal movement

* Increased <u>urinary frequency</u>

* Abdominal <u>pain</u> mimicking <u>labor</u>

* Diagnostics

* Signs and <u>symptoms of pregnancy</u> in absence of <u>gestational sac</u> or fetus on <u>ultrasound</u> and undetectable serum <u>β-hCG</u>

* Diagnostics to identify underlying conditions responsible for signs and <u>symptoms of pregnancy</u>

* Differential diagnosis

* Other psychiatric conditions, e.g., <u>delusion of pregnancy</u> (manifests without objective signs of <u>pregnancy</u>), <u>factitious disorder</u>

* Somatic conditions, e.g., <u>prolactinoma</u>, <u>malignant tumors</u>

* <u>Pregnancy</u>

* Management

* Be sensitive to patient expectations regarding <u>pregnancy</u> and the potential disappointment in receiving the diagnosis.

* See “<u>Approach to patients with suspected somatic symptom and related disorders</u>” for more information.

* Treat underlying conditions (e.g., abdominal distention due to <u>constipation</u>) responsible for signs and symptoms.

* There is no evidence that <u>psychotropic medication</u> is beneficial in treating <u>pseudocyesis</u>.

* Complications: <u>depression</u> due to the unsuccessful attempt to get pregnant





> [!TIP]
> Performing an <u>ultrasound</u> and informing the patient of the results can be both diagnostic and help the patient to accept that they are not pregnant. [[20]](/library/HGcK0V0)

---

## Conditions in which symptoms are consciously generated

* Rarely, patients may intentionally invent or induce symptoms.

* Motivations may vary, e.g., <u>primary gain</u> or <u>secondary gain</u>.

* A diagnosis of a <u>factitious disorder</u> or <u>malingering</u> may be associated with stigma and cause the breakdown of the <u>patient-physician relationship</u>.

* Discuss each case with other involved <u>health care professionals</u>.

* Only apply these diagnoses if they are strongly suspected.

---

## Factitious disorders

See “<u>Medical child abuse</u>” for information on managing victims of <u>factitious disorder imposed on another</u>.




### Overview [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




* Definition: intentional invention or induction of symptoms either in one's self or another person.

* The goal is to get medical attention and sympathy (primary gain) even though the motivation is unconscious.

* Patients are willing to undergo (or allow the person they induce symptoms in) invasive and/or high-risk treatments.

* Characteristic findings

* Deceptive behavior (key feature)

* Impairment related to illness perception and <u>somatization</u> (as in other somatic symptom and related disorders)





> [!TIP]
> In <u>factitious disorders</u>, there is evidence of intentional injury or disease falsification in the absence of <u>external reward</u>, in contrast to <u>somatic symptom disorder</u>, in which there is no evidence of deception, and to <u>malingering</u>, in which <u>external reward</u> is an incentive.




### Comparison of <u>factitious disorder imposed on self</u> versus another




| <br>Comparison of <u>factitious disorders</u> [[23]](/library/0qceCW0) |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Factitious disorder imposed on self | Factitious disorder imposed on another |
| Summary | <br><br>* Previously known as <u>Munchausen syndrome</u><br><br>* Patients intentionally invent or induce physical signs and symptoms, even through self-harm (e.g., by injecting <u>insulin</u>), to assume the role of a patient.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Previously known as <u>Munchausen syndrome by proxy</u><br><br>* Patients intentionally invent or induce symptoms in someone else (usually their child or a disabled or older relative).<br><br>* A type of child or <u>older adult abuse</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Epidemiology</u> | <br><br>* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u><br><br>* Associated with:<br><br>* A history of significant exposure to a health care environment (e.g., profession in health care, significant childhood illness, important relationship with a medical professional)<br><br>* <u>Personality disorders</u> (e.g., <u>narcissistic personality disorder</u>, <u>borderline personality disorder</u>, <u>antisocial personality disorder</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> [[24]](/library/EGc8aV0)<br><br>* Associated with a history of abuse as a child and <u>personality disorders</u> (e.g., <u>narcissistic personality disorder</u>, <u>borderline personality disorder</u>)<br><br>* 1 in 3 patients have a concurrent diagnosis of <u>factitious disorder imposed on self</u>. [[23]](/library/0qceCW0)<br><br><br> |
| Clinical features | <br><br>* History of seeking treatment at numerous different hospitals and/or clinics<br><br>* Resistance when the health care team tries to obtain information from outside sources (e.g., collateral history, notes from another <u>health care system</u>)<br><br>* Atypical illness course and/or atypical organisms found<br><br>* Deterioration predicted or occurs just before discharge.<br><br>* History of nonadherence to treatment and refusing confirmatory diagnostic studies<br><br><br> |  |
| <br><u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria [[1]](/library/Nta-dm) |  |  |
| A | <br>* Intentionally deceptive falsification of disease signs or symptoms, or inducing injury or disease in oneself<br><br> | <br>* Intentionally deceptive falsification of disease signs or symptoms, or inducing injury or disease in another individual<br><br> |
| B | <br>* Present themselves as ill, impaired, or injured to others<br><br> | <br>* Presents the person they induce symptoms in as ill, impaired, or injured to others<br><br> |
| C | <br>* Occurs even in the absence of <u>external rewards</u><br><br> |  |
| D | <br>* Behavior is not better explained by another mental disorder<br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> In <u>factitious disorder imposed on another</u>, the perpetrator receives the diagnosis. An abuse and neglect diagnosis should be considered for the person in whom symptoms have been induced.




### Management [[23]](/library/0qceCW0)




* Provide appropriate care and ensure safety

* Treat any induced illness or injury.

* Avoid unnecessary procedures.

* In whom symptoms have been induced (in <u>factitious disorder imposed on another</u>)

* Provide a safe place away from the perpetrator (e.g., call adult or <u>child protective services</u>).

* Exclude other forms of abuse or neglect if suspected.

* Refer for <u>psychotherapy</u>, depending on the individual's age.

* If it is safe to do so, discuss the diagnosis with the patient in a supportive, nonthreatening manner.  [[7]](/library/5OciGc0)

* Do not discuss the diagnosis with the patient alone; involve a <u>psychiatrist</u>.

* Gather the facts  and establish a strategy that includes continuous patient support and follow-up.

* Document the meeting and the outcome in the patient's records.

* Share information with relevant health care services and agencies.

* If the patient is willing to engage with management:

* Refer for <u>psychotherapy</u> and/or parenting classes.

* Assess for comorbid conditions.

* Monitor pharmacotherapy intake.





> [!TIP]
> Very few patients with a <u>factitious disorder</u> acknowledge their condition and engage in management. [[23]](/library/0qceCW0)




> [!WARNING]
> Involve adult or <u>child protective services</u> if a <u>factitious disorder imposed on another</u> is suspected.

---

## Malingering

### Overview [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)[[23]](/library/0qceCW0)




* The intentional fabrication or exaggeration of symptoms for secondary gain (e.g., time off work, avoiding the police, obtaining narcotics, insurance money) ;  [[23]](/library/0qceCW0)

* Adoption of the sick role may provide the patient with an opportunity to avoid social obligations in a “socially accepted” way.

* Complaints usually stop after the intended <u>external reward</u> has been obtained (as opposed to in <u>factitious disorders</u>).

* <u>Malingering</u> individuals may be uncooperative and may insist on undergoing an extensive medical evaluation.

* Symptoms typically do not conform to a known medical or psychological condition.

* Symptoms are:

* Typically vague and inconsistent

* False or significantly exaggerated

* <u>Malingering</u> is not classified as a mental disorder.





### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[25]](/library/tGcXaV0)

* Often occurs after an accident, particularly if legal proceedings are being started





### Diagnostics [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)




* Any combination of the following is suggestive of <u>malingering</u>: [[1]](/library/Nta-dm)

* The patient presents under medicolegal circumstances (e.g., via <u>self-referral</u> or referral by an attorney while criminal charges are pending).

* Clinical findings are markedly inconsistent with the patient's complaints.

* Lack of patient cooperation during diagnostic evaluation, follow-up, and/or treatment

* Features of <u>antisocial personality disorder</u>

* Consider using screening tools for <u>malingering</u> such as the structured interview of reported symptoms or the Miller forensic assessment of symptom test (M-<u>FAST</u>).  [[26]](/library/xNcEW10)





### Management [[23]](/library/0qceCW0)




* Explain the objective clinical and diagnostic study findings to the patient and make a detailed record in the patient's file.

* Avoid unnecessary referral; , as this perpetuates <u>malingering</u>.

* The diagnosis should only be directly discussed with the patient as part of a supportive confrontation.





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid using the term “<u>malingering</u>” in the patient's medical record. [[23]](/library/0qceCW0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Malingering</u> is not classified as a somatic symptom and related disorder or a mental illness in the <u>DSM-5</u>.

---

## Differential diagnoses

| Differential diagnoses of somatic symptom and related disorders |  |
| --- | --- |
| Disorders | Description |
| <u>Factitious disorder imposed on self</u> | <br><br>* Evidence of intentional production or exaggeration of somatic complaints about oneself<br><br>* No <u>secondary gain</u>; goal is to assume the role of a patient in order to receive sympathy and medical care<br><br>* Medical complaints continue even after medical care has been provided.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Factitious disorder imposed on another</u> | <br><br>* Intentional production or fabrication of symptoms in someone else (usually children/older adults)<br><br>* No <u>secondary gain</u>; goal is to become the caregiver of the patient and gain benefits as a result of that.<br><br>* Complaints continue even after medical care has been provided.<br><br><br> |
| Vulnerable child syndrome | <br><br>* Child is perceived by parents as <u>prone</u> to getting ill or injured<br><br>* Commonly starts after the child experienced serious illness or a life-threatening accident<br><br>* Multiple absences from school and/or exaggerated use of medical services is common<br><br><br> |
| <u>Somatic symptom disorder</u> | <br><br>* Excessive somatic complaints and worry<br><br>* Absence of a serious medical condition<br><br>* No evidence of production or exaggeration of somatic complaints<br><br>* No <u>secondary gain</u><br><br>* Relieved by regularly scheduled appointments and tests<br><br><br> |
| <u>Functional neurological symptom disorder</u> | <br><br>* Calm, indifferent patient<br><br>* Neurological symptoms that are incompatible with recognized neurological or medical conditions<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Malingering</u><br> | <br><br>* Intentionally vague, inconsistent somatic complaints<br><br>* <u>Secondary gain</u> (e.g., to avoid working)<br><br>* Medical complaints stop after the objective of <u>secondary gain</u> has been achieved (e.g., paid medical leave)<br><br><br> |




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.
